domain_description: The classroom formative cycle — setting clear targets, eliciting evidence of learning, diagnosing gaps, and closing them with usable feedback. All interventions cross-referenced to peer-reviewed meta-analyses where one exists, and to the EEF Toolkit where a matching strand exists.

skills.description: Unpack a competency or standard into the underlying knowledge, skills, and observable success criteria students need to demonstrate.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Unpacking standards into success criteria is teacher prep work that can be done once per unit; no new materials, no training beyond awareness, no structural change.

skills.description: Author student-friendly learning targets that tie each target to its broader purpose — what students will be able to do, and why it matters.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Authoring learning targets is teacher prep work done once per lesson or unit; no materials, no training beyond awareness of structure.

skills.description: Design a single multiple-choice question, placed at a hinge point in a lesson, whose distractors diagnose specific misconceptions and tell you whether to move on, pause, or reteach.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Hinge questions take only 1-2 minutes per lesson to deploy, but writing good ones takes real pedagogical content knowledge — distractors must be anchored in actual misconceptions, not generic plausibility, or the question stops diagnosing anything.

skills.description: Design a structured protocol of formative checks across a lesson — cold call, mini-whiteboards, exit tickets, ABCD cards, hand signals — so every student's understanding is sampled before the lesson ends.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Protocol design happens once per unit; the techniques themselves (cold call, mini-whiteboards, exit tickets) need no materials beyond what teachers already have and no training beyond awareness of the technique set.

skills.description: Select the most appropriate formative assessment technique for a specific learning goal, lesson phase, and class context — matching technique to purpose rather than defaulting to one habit.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: A selection task done during lesson planning; the techniques selected from are already part of common teacher repertoire. No materials, training, or structural change required to use the selector itself.

skills.description: Analyse a set of student work for systematic gaps in understanding — patterns, not one-off errors — then translate the patterns into specific next-step teaching moves.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Looking for patterns across a class set takes real time per cycle and benefits from a framework or lens for what to look for; no materials beyond student work, but more cognitive effort than a single check-for-understanding move.

skills.description: Structure how students examine their own and others' errors — identifying what went wrong, why, and what to do differently — so mistakes become deliberate learning material rather than something to hide.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: A protocol used after assessment or practice; takes 10-15 min per session, no materials beyond student work, technique is teachable in a short briefing.

skills.description: Map the typical sequence of how understanding develops in a topic — what students typically know first, what comes next, where the predictable plateaus and misconceptions sit — so teaching, assessment, and feedback can target the right step.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: A unit-design task done once per topic; requires real pedagogical content knowledge to identify prerequisites, predictable misconceptions, and intermediate understandings, but no materials and no training beyond awareness of the construct.

skills.description: Generate a criterion-referenced rubric with explicit performance criteria, distinguishing descriptive language across levels, so students and teachers share a common picture of what quality looks like.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Designing a rubric where each performance level actually distinguishes meaningful difference (not just 'good / OK / poor') takes real work — defining criteria, writing descriptive language for each level. AI generation accelerates but doesn't eliminate the cognitive design work. Once built, the rubric is reusable across cohorts.

skills.description: Design a single-point rubric — one column describing proficient performance, with open spaces for noting 'areas to grow' and 'areas of strength' — for feedback that's faster to write and more growth-oriented than traditional analytic rubrics.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Single-point rubrics are simpler to design than multi-level analytic rubrics — one performance description per criterion. The cost saving over analytic rubrics is real. Teachers can craft them per assignment with no training beyond awareness of the format.
